title: The great holocaust, 1762
hookLine: Ahmad Shah Abdali's army kills a great many Sikhs in a day, then blows up the Harmandir

cards: A winter morning in February, 1762, on the flat farmland southwest of Ludhiana. A long, slow column moves across the fields. Not an army, mostly.
Families. Grandparents on carts, children on their mothers' hips, cooking pots, cattle, everything they own, heading for safety in the dry country to the south. The fighters ride alongside.
And then, on the horizon, dust. An army that had marched through the night. Today: Vadda Ghallughara, the great holocaust.

teach.b: Vadda means great, large. Ghallughara, as you heard a few days ago, means a massacre, a great destruction. The army belonged to Ahmad Shah Abdali, the king of Afghanistan, who invaded northern India many times.
He had marched fast to catch the Sikhs off guard, near the village of Kup. The Sikh fighters did something remarkable.

teach.h: KUP, 1762: A MOVING RING OF FIGHTERS.
teach.b: They formed a moving ring around the families and kept the whole column walking, fighting on the outside while the old and the young moved in the middle, all through the day. But the losses were terrible.
Many thousands were killed in that one day, among them many women, children and old people. The old accounts give numbers from about ten thousand to far more. Nobody knows exactly.
That spring, at Vaisakhi, Abdali came to Amritsar.
His men packed the Harmandir with gunpowder and blew it up, and filled the sacred pool with rubble. It looked like the end. It wasn't.
That same autumn, the Sikhs gathered at Amritsar at Diwali and faced Abdali's army again, and he withdrew.
Within two years they were rebuilding the Harmandir and clearing the pool, brick by brick. Soon after, the Sikhs held Lahore. So the Sikh memory of 1762 has two halves.
One is grief, held carefully and without hatred for anyone living today.
The other is the comeback, told with quiet pride: the panth rose again.

how: Sikhs remember the Vadda Ghallughara each year, especially near Kup-Rahira, where a memorial and gurdwara stand; the rebuilding of the Harmandir after 1764 is remembered as the panth rising again.

games.q: you're a Sikh fighter. an army has caught your column of families in the open. what do you do?
o: form a moving ring around the families and keep walking.
games.why: the fighters ringed the families and kept them moving all day, fighting on the outside.

practice: Breathe slowly. On each in-breath, remember the families in the column, and anyone you know who has lived through loss; on each out-breath, let a little of the weight go, not the memory, just the weight.
If you pray, you can hold them in the prayer you know.

wordCard.voice: Vadda Ghallughara. The great holocaust of 1762, when many thousands of Sikhs were killed in a single day and the Harmandir was destroyed. And the panth rose again.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: vadda, great; ghallughara, a massacre or great destruction.

carryVoice: Your line: the panth rose again. Grief and comeback, both remembered. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.
